client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on my university assignments at all — I'll sit down to study and just end up staring at the wall, feeling this heavy sadness wash over me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that the heavy, foggy grief you're describing after losing your grandmother makes complete sense — loss like that can make even the simplest tasks feel impossibly distant. You're not broken; you're grieving. I'm curious, when you sit down to study and that sadness washes over you, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, a lot of the thoughts are about her — like, I'll suddenly remember that I was supposed to call her more often and I just... didn't. And then I start thinking that I'm a terrible person for letting time slip by like that, and that I don't even deserve to be sitting there trying to get my degree when she never got to see me finish it. It's like guilt just takes over everything and studying feels completely pointless.
therapist: That guilt sounds really crushing — the thought that you "should have" called more, and then punishing yourself so harshly that you feel you don't even deserve your own future. I want to gently ask: do you think your grandmother, knowing you the way she did, would have seen you as a terrible person for the normal, imperfect way life gets busy? What do you imagine she would actually say to you right now, sitting at that desk?

client: I know logically she probably wouldn't have called me a terrible person — she was always so warm and forgiving. But when I try to imagine what she'd say, I just feel this wave of sadness instead of comfort, and then I feel guilty for not being able to hold onto that image of her without falling apart. It's like the exercise you're suggesting sounds nice in theory, but in practice my brain just won't cooperate with it.
therapist: What you're describing is so understandable — grief has a way of making even the most comforting thoughts feel bittersweet and out of reach, and it's not a failure of yours that your brain isn't cooperating right now, it's just how raw this still is. I also want to gently notice something: you're now feeling guilty about *how* you're grieving, on top of the original guilt — like there's a part of you that's holding you to an impossible standard even in your sadness. I wonder, if a close friend came to you feeling exactly what you're feeling right now, would you tell them they were doing grief *wrong*?

client: No, I wouldn't tell a friend they were doing grief wrong — I'd probably just sit with them and tell them it's okay to feel whatever they're feeling. But it's so much harder to apply that to myself, and part of me wonders if I'm just using that logic as a way to let myself off the hook for genuinely neglecting her when she was alive. I guess I don't fully trust that I deserve the same compassion I'd give someone else.
therapist: There's something really important in what you just said — you can clearly see the compassion you'd offer a friend, but there's a quiet, persistent voice telling you that *you specifically* don't deserve it, almost like self-compassion feels like cheating rather than healing. That fear of "letting yourself off the hook" is worth exploring, because there's a difference between genuinely reflecting on a relationship and using guilt as a way to punish yourself indefinitely — one leads to growth, the other just keeps you stuck. Can you tell me a little more about what "genuinely neglecting her" means to you — what would the evidence for and against that really look like if you examined it honestly?

client: When I think about the evidence, I guess the honest truth is that I did visit her last Christmas and I called her on her birthday, but then there were months where I just got caught up in deadlines and didn't reach out at all. The neglect feels real because I knew she was getting older and I still let those months slip by, so it's hard to just dismiss that as nothing. I'm not sure examining the evidence is going to make me feel less guilty — it almost feels like I'm just building a case to excuse myself rather than actually facing what I did.
therapist: You're actually doing something really honest and brave right now — you're not dismissing the months you didn't call, you're holding them alongside the Christmas visit and the birthday call, and that's not building an excuse, that's looking at the *whole* picture rather than just the worst parts. The guilt is telling you to focus only on what you didn't do, but a fair witness to your own life would also have to account for what you *did* do — and the love that was clearly there. I'm curious: do you think it's possible to acknowledge that you weren't perfect at staying in touch, feel genuine sadness about that, *and* still not be someone who neglected her — can those things exist at the same time?

client: I think intellectually I can see that those things could coexist, but emotionally it just doesn't feel that simple — like my feelings aren't catching up with the logic. Part of me is actually a little frustrated because it sounds like you're saying the right things, but I'm sitting here and the guilt still feels just as heavy as when I walked in. I guess I'm wondering how long it takes before any of this actually starts to sink in, because right now it feels like I'm just rearranging words without anything really shifting inside.
therapist: Your frustration is completely valid, and I want to name something important: the fact that the guilt still feels heavy right now isn't a sign that this isn't working — it's a sign that you're dealing with something real and deep that took years to build, and it won't dissolve in a single conversation. The gap between understanding something intellectually and *feeling* it differently is actually one of the most honest things you can experience in this process, and noticing that gap is itself a meaningful step. I'm wondering — when you imagine what "something shifting inside" would actually feel like, what are you hoping for?

client: I think what I'm hoping for is just to be able to sit down at my desk and not immediately feel crushed by her absence — like, to have the sadness be there but not completely swallow me whole so I can still function. I guess I want to feel like I was a decent granddaughter, not just tell myself I was. But even saying that out loud makes me worry that I'm just chasing some feeling that might never actually come, and I'll be stuck in this forever.
therapist: What you just described — sadness that's present but not consuming, and a felt sense of your own worth as a granddaughter — that's not an unrealistic fantasy, that's actually a very achievable and human thing to hope for, and the fact that you can name it so clearly tells me a lot about your self-awareness. The fear of being "stuck forever" is one grief tells almost everyone, but what you're describing sounds less like someone who is stuck and more like someone who is right in the middle of a painful but real process. I want to gently hold onto what you said — that you want to *feel* like a decent granddaughter, not just tell yourself you were — so I'm curious, are there any specific memories of her, moments you shared, that already carry that feeling even a little bit?

client: There's this one memory that keeps coming back to me — she taught me how to make her bread recipe when I was about twelve, and I remember her laughing at how badly I kneaded the dough, but she was so patient and kept guiding my hands. When I think about that, there's this small warm feeling underneath the sadness, like maybe she did know I loved her even when I wasn't calling. But then I almost feel guilty for letting myself feel that warmth, like I don't have the right to hold onto the good memories when I also let her down.
therapist: That memory is so beautiful, and I want you to notice what just happened — you found it yourself, that small warm feeling, which means it's already inside you and it's real. The guilt rushing in to take it away is worth paying attention to, because it's almost like a part of you believes you have to choose between loving her and acknowledging the imperfect parts of the relationship, when actually that bread-making moment *is* the evidence you've been looking for — she knew. What do you think it would mean for your grief if you allowed yourself to hold onto that warmth not as a reward you've earned, but simply as something that's true?

client: I think if I could actually hold onto that warmth as just... true, rather than something I have to earn, it might make the grief feel a little less like a punishment. But I'm honestly not sure how to do that in practice — like, when the guilt rushes in and tries to take it away, I don't know how to stop it from winning. It feels like I'd need to consciously fight for that memory every single time, and I'm already so exhausted.
therapist: The exhaustion you're feeling is so real, and I want to offer a gentle reframe: the goal isn't to *fight* the guilt every time it appears, because that takes enormous energy you don't have right now — it's more about slowly building a habit of *noticing* when the guilt rushes in, almost like watching a wave arrive, without immediately believing everything it tells you. That bread memory doesn't need to defeat the guilt to be true; it just needs to be allowed to exist alongside it, and with practice that becomes less of a battle and more of a quiet returning. I'm wondering — in the coming days, when that memory surfaces, what might it look like to simply let yourself stay with the warmth for just a few seconds before the guilt has a chance to pull you away?

client: I think I could maybe try that — just a few seconds feels less overwhelming than trying to hold onto the warmth indefinitely. But I'm a little worried that even attempting it will feel forced or artificial, like I'm performing grief correctly instead of actually feeling it. I guess what I'm asking is, how do I know if I'm genuinely staying with the warmth versus just going through the motions because a therapist told me to?
therapist: That question itself is actually your answer — someone just going through the motions wouldn't stop to ask whether it was genuine, they'd simply perform it and move on, but you're already bringing a real, searching honesty to this. The warmth you felt remembering the bread-making wasn't something I suggested to you; it arose on its own when you found that memory, which means it belongs to you, not to any technique. I think the truest measure of whether you're genuinely with it versus performing it is simply — does it feel like *her*, even for a moment?
